      <title>[Editorial] Digital technology for health, not harm</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01991-4/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>Few who remember the idealistic vision of the 1990s World Wide Web could have anticipated the extent to which the internet would reshape modern life. Today's children have never lived in a world without smartphones and ubiquitous digital connectivity, and must contend with online shaming and bullying, permanent digital footprints, and weaponised attention economies. Generative artificial intelligence can now detach us from reality, providing emotional support and companionship for some, while supplying our most personal disclosures to trillion-dollar tech companies.</description>
      <dc:title>Digital technology for health, not harm</dc:title>

      <title>[Comment] Mitapivat in the RISE UP trial: a new therapy for sickle cell disease</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)02046-5/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>Sickle cell disease is the most common haemoglobinopathy, affecting more than 7 million people worldwide.1 Despite substantial morbidity and mortality, access to effective disease-modifying therapies remains limited.2,3 Hydroxyurea and chronic blood transfusions have both been shown to reduce acute sickle cell disease complications, including vaso-occlusive crises and stroke, while also improving haematological parameters.4,5 However, the availability and long-term feasibility of both could be limited in some settings.</description>

      <title>[Comment] Deucrictibant: a novel oral on-demand treatment for hereditary angioedema</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01855-6/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>Hereditary angioedema due to a deficiency of C1 inhibitor (HAE-C1INH) is clinically characterised by recurrent, generally unpredictable attacks of angioedema.1 Untreated episodes are often severe and prolonged, lasting up to 3–5 days and engendering considerable morbidity and even mortality.2 Unlike angioedema associated with mast cell mediators, the swelling in HAE-C1INH does not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids, or epinephrine.</description>

      <title>[Comment] Conversational diagnostic AI in primary care: what happens after it speaks?</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01763-0/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>Patients increasingly use conversational artificial intelligence (AI), including for possible diagnoses, before seeing a clinician. However, clinical evidence is lacking and is mostly synthetic. The Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), for example, outperformed primary care physicians in text consultations, but its patients were patient actors.1 One exception is a randomised trial of 2069 patients in which a chatbot generated histories, preliminary diagnoses, and test orders, sometimes without staff support, although its primary outcomes focused mainly on efficiency.</description>
      <dc:title>Conversational diagnostic AI in primary care: what happens after it speaks?</dc:title>

      <title>[Comment] The US opioid epidemic at a turning point</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01610-7/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>After more than a decade of rising mortality, the USA is experiencing an unexpected and encouraging decline in drug overdose deaths. According to provisional estimates from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately 70 000 people died from drug overdoses in 2025—nearly 14% fewer than in 2024, marking the third consecutive annual decline, from a high of almost 108 000 in 2022.1,2 The reduction in overdose deaths has been widespread, as nearly every state in the country reported fewer overdose deaths in 2025 compared with the previous year.</description>
      <dc:title>The US opioid epidemic at a turning point</dc:title>

      <description>The psychoanalyst and paediatrician Donald Winnicott proposed that a child discovers his or her own self through creative play.       <title>[Series] The digital determinants of health: a new era for global public health</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01292-4/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>Digital transformations exert increasing influence over the lives of the global population, shaping opportunities and generating harms for health and wellbeing across the spectrum of digital access and engagement. The scale of influence of digital transformations on human and planetary health marks the urgency of attention to the digital determinants of health (DDoH). In this Series paper, we describe a prevailing digital sociotechnological order (DSTO) as the structural source of the DDoH. The DSTO is composed of a set of dominant assumptions that motivate digital practices operating through four features (political norms, economic logics, infrastructures, and personal and social practices) to affect human and planetary health.</description>

      <description>Children and adolescents are growing up in a hybrid world in which digital media has become part of the infrastructure of everyday life and a structural determinant of their health.    <item rdf:about="https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01293-6/fulltext?rss=yes">
      <title>[Series] Governing the digital determinants of health for children and young people: a global public health imperative</title>
      <link>https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01293-6/fulltext?rss=yes</link>
      <description>The digital determinants of health are the structural conditions through which digital infrastructures, business models, and design choices shape health outcomes. Yet these determinants remain largely outside public health policy and remain fragmented across regulatory sectors. Rather than regulating individual technologies in isolation, governance should ensure that digital systems and environments advance population health and reduce inequities. A public health approach shifts attention from individual responsibility—and the tendency to blame users—towards the governance of the structural features that produce health risks and inequities.</description>
